## Introduction

The public health institute of Sweway is investigating an outbreak of influenza
in the country. This document is a worked example of using the `seirvax` package
to simulate the spread of the disease and to evaluate potential intervention
strategies. It follows the course an investigation might take: looking at the
early case data, estimating how fast the outbreak is growing, building a
transmission model, fitting it to what has been observed, and projecting
forward under different measures.

All information in this document is fake and intended for a pandemic
preparedness exercise. Sweway is one of four fictional countries bundled with
the package, each with five regions and population by five-year age band.

This document works end to end on one outbreak. The scripts in `examples/`
take the same features one at a time, and are the place to look for the
details behind each step:

| | |
|---|---|
| `01_single_population.R` | one population, deterministic and stochastic runs, plot styles |
| `02_age_structured.R` | age mixing, susceptibility, severity and vaccine effectiveness by age |
| `03_age_and_region.R` | combining age and region mixing, seeding, interventions over time |
| `04_scenarios.R` | comparing several scenarios with `compare_scenarios()` |
| `05_fitting.R` | the three fitting methods, priors, diagnostics and projections |
| `06_country_data.R` | the bundled country data, distances and maps |
| `07_line_list_exercise.R` | generating exercise data and fitting R0 back from it |

`docs/model_description.md` has the equations and assumptions, and
`docs/data.md` describes the bundled data. The exercise uses the following
geographical data:

```{r}
#| label: fig-geographical-data
#| fig-cap: "The regions of Sweway and its neighbours, shaded by population."
library(seirvax)   # devtools::load_all() instead when working on the package

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

plot_region_map()
```

## Early outbreak

Early in an outbreak the available data is thin. Here it is a line list of
around 650 individual cases: everyone admitted to hospital or who died, plus a
fraction of the milder infections that happened to be detected. Each row is one
case, with the dates of symptom onset, hospital admission and death where they
apply, along with the patient's age group and region.

```{r}
#| label: line-list
ll <- simulate_line_list(t_max = 30, n_seed = 30, R0 = 1.4)
head(ll)
```

`simulate_line_list()` is what the organisers use to produce the data; its
arguments — the disease's natural history, severity by age, vaccination
coverage, how many infections are detected — are shown in
`examples/07_line_list_exercise.R`.

Counting cases by onset date gives the epidemic curve so far:

```{r}
#| label: fig-epi-curve
#| fig-cap: "Detected cases by date of symptom onset."
ll %>% group_by(date_onset) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date_onset, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

### Growth rate

Before building a transmission model, a simple regression tells us how fast the
outbreak is growing. Hospital admissions are the most reliable series in the
line list, since every admission is detected, so we fit a Poisson regression of
daily admissions against date. The coefficient on date is the exponential
growth rate, and `log(2)` divided by it is the doubling time.

```{r}
#| label: fig-poisson
#| fig-cap: "Daily hospital admissions with the fitted exponential growth and a 95% prediction interval extrapolated three weeks ahead."
hosp_inc <- as.data.frame(ll %>% filter(hospitalised == TRUE) %>%
                            group_by(date_hospital) %>% summarise(I = n()))

fit <- glm(I ~ date_hospital, data = hosp_inc, family = poisson)
summary(fit)

ci <- confint(fit)[2, ]
print(glue::glue("Growth rate estimate: {round(coef(fit)[2], 3)} ",
                 "(95% CI: {round(ci[1], 3)} - {round(ci[2], 3)})"))
print(glue::glue("Doubling time estimate: {round(log(2) / coef(fit)[2], 3)} days"))

preds <- ciTools::add_pi(
  data.frame(date_hospital = hosp_inc$date_hospital[1] + 1:(nrow(hosp_inc) + 3 * 7),
             I = 0),
  fit = fit, level = 0.95, names = c("lwr", "upr"))

ggplot(hosp_inc, aes(x = date_hospital, y = I)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict(fit, type = "response")), color = "red") +
  geom_ribbon(data = preds, aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.2)
```

This extrapolation assumes the growth continues unchanged, which is only
reasonable for a short horizon: it has no way to represent the depletion of
susceptible people, nor the effect of any measures taken. That is what the
transmission model below is for.

### Who is affected

The line list also shows which age groups and regions the cases are in. This
matters both for targeting measures and, later, for checking whether the model's
assumptions about severity and mixing are plausible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-region
#| fig-cap: "Detected cases by age group and by region."
ll %>% group_by(age_group) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

ll %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

## Simulating an influenza outbreak with seirvax

`examples/01_single_population.R` and `examples/02_age_structured.R` build up
the same model step by step, with more detail on each argument.

A model needs to know how many people there are, how they are grouped, and how
they mix. We start by defining the population matrix for Sweway and a social
contact matrix. For now we treat the country as a single population, with four
age groups.

Population matrix:

```{r}
#| label: population
N <- population_matrix("Sweway", age_breaks = c(0, 20, 45, 65), by_region = FALSE)
N
```

Mixing matrix: the number of contacts per day between age groups. There is no
contact survey for Sweway, so we borrow the POLYMOD survey from the United
Kingdom, aggregated to the same four age groups.


```{r}
#| label: mixing
library(socialmixr)
M <- contact_matrix(polymod, countries = "United Kingdom",
                    age.limits = c(0, 20, 45, 65), symmetric = TRUE)
M$matrix
```

With the population and mixing matrices in hand we can build a model. Besides
those, it needs the natural history of the disease (how long people are latent
and infectious), how likely each age group is to be hospitalised, and how many
infections to start with.

```{r}
#| label: fig-first-run
#| fig-cap: "Hospital occupancy over 30 days, 100 stochastic simulations."
#| echo: true
model <- build_model(N = N, R0 = 1.5, C_age = M$matrix,
                     p_hosp = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1),
                     latent_period = 1, infectious_period = 2, I0 = 20)

res <- run_model(model, "stochastic", t_max = 30, n_sim = 100)
plot(res, var = "H")
```

### Fitting R0 to the observed admissions

`examples/05_fitting.R` covers the fitting machinery in more depth: what each
method does, how to change the priors, trace plots and other diagnostics, and
what the uncertainty in a projection does and does not include.

Rather than guessing R0, we can estimate it from the observed admissions using
the same model. Two methods are shown: `optim`, which gives a quick point
estimate, and `pmcmc`, which runs a particle filter so that the estimate
accounts for the randomness of the epidemic as well as the noise in the data.

Note that we have assumed values for `I0` and `p_hosp`, and that these will
obviously affect the fit: a model that assumes a lower probability of
hospitalisation needs more infections, and so a higher R0, to produce the same
number of admissions.

```{r}
#| label: fitting
data <- hosp_inc %>%
  mutate(time = as.numeric(date_hospital - min(date_hospital)) + 1,
         admissions = I) %>%
  select(time, admissions)

observed_age_dist <- ll[hospitalised == TRUE,
                        .N, by = .(band = cut(age_mid, c(0, 20, 45, 65, Inf),
                                              right = FALSE,
                                              labels = c("0-19", "20-44",
                                                         "45-64", "65+")))]
observed_region_dist <- ll[hospitalised == TRUE, .N, by = .(region)]

fit1 <- fit_model(model, data, pars = "R0", method = "optim")
fit1

fit3 <- fit_model(model, data, pars = "R0", method = "pmcmc",
                  n_steps = 300, n_chains = 1, n_particles = 100, dt = 0.25,
                  n_threads = 4, seed = 1)
fit3
```

The fitted model can be compared with the data it was fitted to, and with the
age distribution of admissions, which the fit never saw:

```{r}
#| label: fig-fit
#| fig-cap: "The fitted model against the observed admissions."
plot(fit3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-fit-age
#| fig-cap: "Modelled hospital admissions by age group (points and intervals) against the observed numbers (red)."
plot(fit3, type = "distribution", by = "age", measure = "cum_hosp") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = band, y = N, ymin = N, ymax = N),
                data = observed_age_dist, color = "red")

# plot(fit3, type = "distribution", by = "region", measure = "cum_hosp") +
#   geom_errorbar(aes(x = region, y = N, ymin = N, ymax = N),
#                 data = observed_region_dist, color = "red")
```

The match is poor, because of the assumed values for the hospitalisation
probabilities and the borrowed age-based mixing matrix. Fitting R0 pins down how
fast the epidemic grows, but it cannot correct the age pattern: that comes
entirely from `p_hosp` and the contact matrix. Improving it means revisiting
those assumptions rather than the fit.

## Scenarios

`examples/04_scenarios.R` compares a set of scenarios in a few lines, and
`examples/03_age_and_region.R` shows the difference between scaling contacts
with `beta_schedule` and changing the mixing pattern with `mixing_schedule`.

With a fitted model we can project forward and ask what different measures would
do. Projections start where the data ends and carry the fit's uncertainty: each
posterior draw is run separately, and for a `pmcmc` fit each one continues from
the state the particle filter reached, so the projection follows the epidemic
that was actually observed.

The baseline is the fitted model with nothing changed:

```{r}
#| label: fig-baseline
#| fig-cap: "Projected daily hospital admissions under the baseline, one line per posterior draw."
proj <- project_fit(fit3, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50)
plot(proj, var = "inc_hosp")
```

The first scenario reduces contacts across the board by 30% from day 40, as a
broad distancing measure would:

```{r}
#| label: fig-lockdown
#| fig-cap: "Projection with contacts reduced by 30% from day 40."
lockdown <- update_model(fit3$model,
                         beta_schedule = data.frame(time = 40, mult = 0.7))

proj2 <- project_fit(fit3, model = lockdown, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50)
plot(proj2, var = "inc_hosp")

comp <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj, lockdown = proj2))
plot(comp, var = "inc_hosp", style = "spaghetti")
```

The second scenario leaves the overall contact rate alone and changes who meets
whom: contacts involving the over-65s are halved from day 40, as shielding of
the most vulnerable group would. This is a change to the mixing matrix rather
than a multiplier on transmission.

```{r}
#| label: fig-protect-elderly
#| fig-cap: "Projection with contacts involving the over-65s halved from day 40, and all three scenarios together."
protect_elderly_mm <- M$matrix
protect_elderly_mm[, 4] <- protect_elderly_mm[, 4] * 0.5
protect_elderly_mm[4, 1:3] <- protect_elderly_mm[4, 1:3] * 0.5

model_protect_elderly <- update_model(
  fit3$model,
  mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 40, C_age = protect_elderly_mm)))

proj3 <- project_fit(fit3, model = model_protect_elderly, t_max = 100,
                     n_draws = 50)

comp2 <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj, lockdown = proj2,
                                protect_elderly = proj3))
plot(comp2, var = "inc_hosp", style = "spaghetti")
```

Finally, the total number of hospital admissions under each scenario, with the
uncertainty carried through from the fit:

```{r}
#| label: scenario-totals
summary(comp2)[measure == "cum_hosp"]
```

## Adding regions

`examples/03_age_and_region.R` sets out the age × region structure, and
`examples/06_country_data.R` covers the bundled population data, the distances
between regions and the maps.

So far the whole country has been treated as one well-mixed population. The line
list, though, records which region each case is in, and the outbreak clearly did
not start everywhere at once. A regional model lets us ask where hospital
pressure will fall, and whether restricting travel between regions would help.

The population matrix now keeps the regions instead of pooling them, giving one
column per region:

```{r}
#| label: population-regions
N_reg <- population_matrix("Sweway", age_breaks = c(0, 20, 45, 65))
N_reg
```

We also need to say how much people mix between regions. There is no travel
survey for Sweway, so we assume that most contacts happen at home and that the
rest fall off with distance between the regional centres. Two numbers carry the
assumption: the share of contacts made in a person's own region, and the
distance scale over which the remainder spreads.

```{r}
#| label: region-mixing
dist <- region_distances(country = "Sweway")
round(dist)

within <- 0.95        # share of contacts made in the home region
scale_km <- 100       # distance scale for the rest

w <- exp(-dist / scale_km)
diag(w) <- 0
M_region <- (1 - within) * w / rowSums(w)
diag(M_region) <- within
round(M_region, 3)
```

### Where the outbreak started

In the national model it was enough to say how many infections to start with. With
regions we have to say *where* they were, and that choice drives the whole
regional picture. The line list tells us: the region with the earliest onsets,
and the most cases in the first days, is where the outbreak took hold first.

```{r}
#| label: seeding
first_cases <- ll[, .(first_onset = min(date_onset),
                      early_cases = sum(date_onset < min(ll$date_onset) + 10),
                      total = .N), by = region][order(first_onset, -early_cases)]
first_cases

seed_region <- as.character(first_cases$region[1])

# all initial infections in working-age adults in that region, and nowhere else
I0_reg <- matrix(0, nrow(N_reg), ncol(N_reg), dimnames = dimnames(N_reg))
I0_reg["20-44", seed_region] <- 30
I0_reg
```

### Fitting the regional model

The model is built exactly as before, with the region mixing matrix and the
explicit seeding added. We fit R0 to the same national admissions series, so the
regional distribution is something the fit never sees and can be used to check
the travel assumption.

```{r}
#| label: fit-regions
model_reg <- build_model(N = N_reg, R0 = 1.5, C_age = M$matrix,
                         M_region = M_region,
                         p_hosp = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1),
                         latent_period = 1, infectious_period = 2, I0 = I0_reg)

fit_reg <- fit_model(model_reg, data, pars = "R0", method = "pmcmc",
                     n_steps = 300, n_chains = 1, n_particles = 100, dt = 0.25,
                     n_threads = 4, seed = 1)
fit_reg
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-region-dist
#| fig-cap: "Modelled hospital admissions by region over the period covered by the data (points and intervals) against the observed numbers (red)."
observed_region_dist <- ll[hospitalised == TRUE, .N, by = .(region)]

plot(fit_reg, type = "distribution", by = "region", measure = "cum_hosp") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = region, y = N, ymin = N, ymax = N),
                data = observed_region_dist, color = "red")

project_summary(fit_reg, by = "region", t_max = max(data$time),
                measures = "cum_hosp", n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
```

The model concentrates admissions in the seeded region more than the data does,
while the other regions lag behind. That is a statement about the travel
assumption rather than about R0: with only 5% of contacts made outside the home
region, the epidemic spreads between regions more slowly than it evidently did.
Raising `within`'s complement, or shortening the distance scale, would spread it
faster. The regional distribution is for the travel assumption what the age
distribution was for the hospitalisation probabilities.

### Scenario: restricting travel between regions

The natural question for a regional model is whether cutting travel helps. We
reduce cross-regional contacts five-fold from day 40 by swapping in a mixing
matrix with a higher share of contacts at home, and for contrast impose the same
restriction immediately, at the end of the data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-travel-restriction
#| fig-cap: "Daily hospital admissions under the baseline and under reduced travel between all regions, imposed immediately or from day 40."
restricted <- function(within) {
  m <- (1 - within) * w / rowSums(w)
  diag(m) <- within
  m
}

day40 <- update_model(fit_reg$model,
                      mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 40,
                                                  M_region = restricted(0.99))))
immediate <- update_model(fit_reg$model,
                          mixing_schedule = list(list(time = max(data$time),
                                                      M_region = restricted(0.99))))

proj_reg <- project_fit(fit_reg, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
proj_day40 <- project_fit(fit_reg, model = day40, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50,
                          seed = 1)
proj_now <- project_fit(fit_reg, model = immediate, t_max = 100, n_draws = 50,
                        seed = 1)

comp_reg <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = proj_reg,
                                   restrict_day_40 = proj_day40,
                                   restrict_now = proj_now))
plot(comp_reg, var = "inc_hosp")
summary(comp_reg)[measure == "cum_hosp"]
```

Neither restriction makes much difference, and that is the point. By the end of
the data every region already has its own established epidemic, so almost all
transmission is within regions and there is little left for a travel restriction
to prevent. Travel measures matter while an outbreak is still confined to where
it started, and in this outbreak that window closed in the first three weeks,
before our data even ended.

### What if one region had been cut off early?

To see what travel restrictions can do, they have to be in place before the
region is seeded. That cannot be a projection: projections start from the state
at the end of the data, which already has the epidemic everywhere. Instead we
re-run the fitted model from day 0 under a different travel assumption, and
compare it with the fitted baseline.

We isolate the region furthest from where the outbreak started, cutting its
contacts with every other region to a hundredth of normal. Rows of a mixing
matrix have to sum to 1, so the matrix is renormalised afterwards.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isolate-region
#| fig-cap: "Daily hospital admissions by region, with and without one region cut off from the start."
isolate_region <- function(M, region, factor = 0.01) {
  other <- setdiff(rownames(M), region)
  M[region, other] <- M[region, other] * factor
  M[other, region] <- M[other, region] * factor
  M / rowSums(M)                       # rows must still sum to 1
}

far_region <- names(which.max(dist[seed_region, ]))
far_region

isolated <- update_model(
  fit_reg$model,
  mixing_schedule = list(list(time = 0,
                              M_region = isolate_region(M_region, far_region))))

comp_iso <- compare_scenarios(list(baseline = fit_reg$model, isolated = isolated),
                              t_max = 250)
plot(comp_iso, var = "inc_hosp", by = "region")
```

```{r}
#| label: isolate-summary
dcast(summary(comp_iso, by = "region")[measure %in% c("cum_hosp", "peak_hosp_day",
                                                      "peak_hosp_occupancy")],
      region + measure ~ scenario, value.var = "value")
```

The effect falls on that region alone: its epidemic is delayed by weeks and its
peak is slightly lower, while the other regions are unchanged. What isolation
does not do is reduce the total number of admissions there. Once even a handful
of infections get through, a region with R0 above one has its own epidemic, and
that epidemic reaches much the same final size whenever it starts. Cutting
travel buys time — to prepare hospitals, or to vaccinate — rather than
preventing cases, and it only buys time if it is in place before the virus
arrives.
